apps/camera.title: Camera
apps/camera.about:
The computer's camera in a window, and photos taken with it

the computer's camera in a window: the live picture, Take Photo (space, or the button) to keep one in ~/Pictures/Camera, and Record (r) to keep the picture as a film in ~/Videos/Camera, with the microphone's sound where one answers and without it where none does. ffmpeg reads the camera -- video4linux on Linux, AVFoundation on a Mac -- and streams it down a pipe into a media player, the path a film takes, so the picture moves at the camera's own rate. A machine with two cameras, or one that lists a metadata node beside its picture, is tried device by device until one gives a frame; the Camera menu chooses among them and among the sizes the camera says it offers, and the size chosen is kept for next time.

apps/stickies.about:
Notes stuck on the desktop, each its own colour

notes stuck on the desktop, as many as you like, each its own colour, each saved as you type. Launching Stickies opens every note there is (a first, empty one if there are none); the Note menu makes a new one, changes the colour, and deletes one. Closing a note only puts it away until Stickies is opened again -- it is still there.

apps/boxer.about:
DOS games, one folder to a game, in the way Boxer keeps them on a Mac. This window is for getting a game in. Drop a folder, a zip, a disc image or a program on it, or choose one with Import, and it is made into a NAME.boxer the way Boxer does it: an installer is run first, from the game's disc as D:.

apps/bricks.title: Bricks
apps/bricks.about:
Knock the wall down

a bat, a ball and a wall to knock down, after Arkanoid.

Each row of the wall is a string of 1s and 0s, one per brick.  The ball moves one row and one or two columns a step, and takes the columns one at a time, so it never passes through the corner of a brick.  Where it lands on the bat decides how steeply it leaves: the ends send it off at a slant, and the middle sends it back the way it came.

apps/mines.title: Mines
apps/mines.about:
Clear the field without stepping on anything.

The board is three strings of one character per cell: where the mines are, how many touch each cell, and what the player has seen. apps/snake.title: Snake
apps/snake.about:
Eat, grow, and do not bite yourself.

The snake is a string of "row,col" cells, head first.  A step puts a new head on the front and, unless it has just eaten, takes the tail off the back; running into itself is a pattern match on that string.  No arrays, no C: a game written in the shell, stepping on $EPOCHREALTIME.

apps/browser.title: Browser
apps/browser.about:
The web, in a window: a browser engine driven by the web module (a headless Chromium, or WPE WebKit from hibr-browser), each page drawn as cells -- its text where the browser laid it out, in its colours, over a half-block picture of its backgrounds and images. Links are followed with a click, fields typed into, pages scrolled with the wheel or the page keys.

A tab strip along the top -- a click switches, x closes, + opens another -- then back, forward, reload and the address: what is typed there is gone to as it is, with https:// put in front of a bare name, or searched for when it is not an address at all (BW_SEARCH). f6 or ctrl-l puts the keyboard in it; enter goes, escape gives it back to the page. Every other key goes to the page, except one the desktop holds.
apps/browser.author: Omar Sakka
apps/browser.name: browser

apps/mail.title: Mail
apps/mail.about:
Email, offline, labels and conversations as Gmail has them

email in a window, laid out as Gmail lays it out: a search bar, the labels down the side with their unread counts, the conversations in a list -- the sender, the subject and a snippet, the date -- and a conversation opened in place, each message's text drawn from its HTML by the html module, its attached pictures by the img module. Gmail's keys work: j and k move, o or enter opens, u goes back, e archives, # deletes, s stars, I and U mark read and unread, l labels, v moves, c composes, r and a reply and reply to all, f forwards, / searches, and g then i, s, t, d or a goes to the inbox, starred, sent, drafts or all mail.

Everything is kept offline, per account, under ~/.local/share/hibr/mail/ACCOUNT -- msgs.db and the messages themselves -- by lib/mailsync.hibr, run in the background; a second job waits in IMAP IDLE and starts a sync the moment something arrives. What is done here is done to the copy at once and queued for the server, which the next sync brings it to. Accounts are the email module's (~/.config/hibr/mail, readable only by you), set up in Control Panel > Mail; a Google account uses an app password.

apps/diagram.title: Diagram
apps/diagram.about:
A Mermaid diagram editor: the text, and the diagram

a Mermaid diagram editor: the text on one side, the drawing on the other, each following the other as it changes.

The editor half is widgets/textarea.hibr as it comes -- a buffer, a cursor, a selection, undo and the clipboard -- and the drawing half is mods/mermaid, which answers with the text of every row and the style of every character in it as runs. widgets/putruns.hibr draws those with a pen a letter, so the diagram is in the window's own theme colours and nothing here parses an escape sequence. apps/pdfr.about:
A PDF reader: pages as pictures where the terminal can, text where it cannot

a PDF reader (Gitea #348). The document is one continuous column of pages: the wheel, the arrows, page up and down and the scroll bar move through it, and a view that spans the foot of one page and the head of the next is one picture. Fit Width is where a document opens; Fit Page, and zoom in and out, are on the View menu and on w, f, + and -. / searches the whole document, n and N step through what it found, each marked on its page. o shows the contents beside the pages; a link on a page is followed by clicking it -- to its page, or an address to the Browser. apps/write.about:

a word processor for markdown, after MacWrite: what you write is shown as it will read -- headings large, bold bold, italic italic, lists with their bullets, quotes with their bar, code shaded, links underlined, rules drawn -- and only the line the cursor is on shows its markdown, the marks dimmed, so it can always be edited exactly. apps/video.title: Video Player
apps/video.about:
Video Player, every site in one player

every video site in one player: YouTube, Tubi, Bilibili and the ones a lib of the catalogue adds (kind `lib`, `lib/video-<site>`). One list (the site's popular or home page, a search, the history, the favourites), one player (the picture drawn as cells or pixels and the sound through the machine's own device, a bar, a clock, resume, the parts of a video, the next one), one set of menus and keys, whichever site a title is from.

Nothing here is a client of a site. The site's own page runs in the web module's WebKit engine, which fetches, decodes and plays the video itself; the page the video is in is drawn here and this app drives its one <video>: play and pause, a time, the volume. apps/calendar.about:
Your calendars, a month at a time, kept offline from CalDAV

your calendars, kept on this machine from a CalDAV server (Nextcloud, Fastmail, iCloud, Radicale, anything standard): a month at a time, each day's events in it, and the chosen day's events listed underneath; or an agenda of what is coming. The servers are Contacts' -- Control Panel > PIM -- and lib/pimsync.hibr keeps their calendars under ~/.local/share/hibr/pim/SERVER: each event's file, and every occurrence from a year back to two years on, which this reads by date. apps/switchboard.title: Switchboard
apps/switchboard.about:
Watch a longwire switchboard: who is on it and who is ringing whom

a window on a longwire switchboard you run: how many nodes are on it, which of them are online, and who is ringing whom right now. It reads the switchboard's own worker through `lw`, once a second, and follows its event stream for the calls. It watches; it does not decide anything (a ring and a registration are the script's to answer, and the script has two seconds). The head says what this switchboard is and whether anything needs looking at (a key cut to 30 characters says neither): its short code, how long it has been up, its policy and version, how full it is, and a line for what is wrong. Its full address, which a node's `--switchboard HOST:PORT/ADDRESS` needs, is one key away (a, or Node > Copy Switchboard Address). `m` makes the head compact: no graphs, one line for the rest (docs/adr/0075).

Traffic in and out, the calls since it started, and the bans are on its head; `/` searches the nodes by number or name, `o` shows only those online, `b` turns the list into the bans (and `x` lifts one, for the switchboard's owner). Every key is in the menus (docs/adr/0049).

apps/wiretap.about:
Wiretap: a live graph and every app's traffic

system/about.title: About This Computer
system/about.about:
About this computer: the machine, and the desktop running on it

what this is, and what it is running on.

On Linux the machine's own numbers come from /proc, read directly and costing no fork, the same way mods/sysinfo does in C. Nothing else keeps a /proc, so everywhere else forks a system command instead -- vm_stat and sysctl for memory, top for CPU, both throttled to AB_SLOWMS since forking a command every frame is not something to do at DT_TICK's pace. A window rather than the one-line note it used to be, because a bar that means something has to keep being redrawn, and a note fades on its own.

system/tasks.title: Task Manager
system/tasks.about:
What is running, and a way to end one of them.

control-panel/displays.title: Displays
control-panel/displays.about: Control Panel's own picture of a multi-monitor arrangement: a dropdown to choose which display is primary, and every attached display drawn to scale below it from hold clients, dragged to reposition (hold move on release). The primary display is the picture's own anchor -- every rectangle is positioned relative to it, so switching which one is primary, or dragging a *different* display, never moves where the primary itself draws -- but its own rectangle cannot be dragged: the dropdown is the one reliable way to change it, since a mouse click precise enough to land on a specific terminal cell with *no* movement at all is not something to depend on, over ssh least of all. lib/video-bilibili.title: video-bilibili
lib/video-bilibili.about:
Video: Bilibili, a site for the Video player

Bilibili (bilibili.com) for the Video player (apps/video): what only Bilibili knows. A provider lib (kind `lib`): it adds itself to VIDEO_SITES, and the app calls its functions by their prefix, vb_. Bilibili's lists are its own public pages of data (the popular list, a search), which the engine loads like any page and the app reads, after one visit to the site in the window (a search is refused without its cookies). A video is looked up in two steps -- its part, then its file, an MP4 of 720p or 360p that expires, so it is asked for each time one starts -- and played in a small page of this lib's own with one <video> in it. A file the engine cannot reach or play never says so (it stalls): the player gives a title up after thirty seconds. Only ids that look like Bilibili's (BV and letters and digits) are played.
lib/video-bilibili.author: Omar Sakka
lib/video-bilibili.name: video-bilibili

lib/video-bilibilitv.title: video-bilibilitv
lib/video-bilibilitv.about:

A provider lib (kind `lib`): it adds itself to VIDEO_SITES, and the app calls its functions by their prefix, vq_. Its lists (the home page, a search) are the site's own pages, read from their links: a title's id is the number in the link and its words are its picture's text. A video is looked up in one step, the site's own data service (the page the site's player asks it for, loaded in the player tab as a page and read): it answers with the address of an MP4 file, which is played in a small page of this lib's own with one <video> in it. (The site's own player, in a window that is not shown, does not start; the file itself plays and seeks.) A file that does not come is given up on by the player after twenty-five seconds, one that does not play after thirty, and the window says so. Only ids that are numbers are played.

what the video apps (YouTube, Tubi, Bilibili, and the ones after them) share: the history and favourites files, the line of the shared video library (docs/video-library.md of the catalogue), the reading of a line, and a time as 1:05. A library of the catalogue (kind `lib`): installed to <scope>/lib/videocore.hibr, read by the desktop at start (it is chosen by the line below), and named by an app with `# needs: lib/videocore`. boxer.about:
DOS games, one folder to a game, in the way Boxer keeps them on a Mac. mail.about:

Everything is kept offline, per account, under ~/.local/share/hibr/mail/ACCOUNT -- msgs.db and the messages themselves -- by lib/mailsync.hibr, run in the background; a second job waits in IMAP IDLE and starts a sync the moment something arrives. What is done here is done to the copy at once and queued for the server, which the next sync brings it to. video.about:
Video Player, every site in one player

every video site in one player: YouTube, Tubi, Bilibili and the ones a lib of the catalogue adds (kind `lib`, `lib/video-<site>`). One list (the site's popular or home page, a search, the history, the favourites), one player (the picture drawn as cells or pixels and the sound through the machine's own device, a bar, a clock, resume, the parts of a video, the next one), one set of menus and keys, whichever site a title is from.

Nothing here is a client of a site. The site's own page runs in the web module's WebKit engine, which fetches, decodes and plays the video itself; the page the video is in is drawn here and this app drives its one <video>: play and pause, a time, the volume. What only a site knows -- the address of a list, how to read it, how to start a title, what to say to its player -- is its provider's (`lib/video-<site>`, which adds itself to VIDEO_SITES and whose functions this app calls by their prefix). The shared core (lib/videocore) keeps the history, favourites and library lines.
video.author: Omar Sakka
video.name: video

archives.title: Archives
archives.about:
Show archives as folders in Files, compress and extract them

an archive in Files is a folder (Gitea #475, ADR 0053).

A catalogue extension: it opens no window of its own. It registers a location, archive://FILE/path, which Files shows read-only, an opener that sends an archive there, and the verbs Compress, Extract Here and Extract To. Removed, an archive is a plain file again and Files is exactly as it was: Files names none of this.
archives.author: Omar Sakka
archives.name: archives

calendar.title: Calendar
calendar.about:
Your calendars, a month at a time, kept offline from CalDAV

your calendars, kept on this machine from a CalDAV server (Nextcloud, Fastmail, iCloud, Radicale, anything standard): a month at a time, each day's events in it, and the chosen day's events listed underneath; or an agenda of what is coming. The arrows choose a day, n and p (or page down and up) change month, t comes back to today, a and m switch to the agenda and back, tab moves between the month and the day's list, c makes an event on the chosen day, enter makes one there or edits the one chosen in the list, # removes it, R syncs now.

The servers are Contacts' -- Control Panel > PIM -- and lib/pimsync.hibr keeps their calendars under ~/.local/share/hibr/pim/SERVER: each event's file, and every occurrence from a year back to two years on, which this reads by date. A change made here is queued and sent at the next sync. Reminders go off whether or not a Calendar window is open: a ticker run after every frame looks for the next one and asks for the frame it is due in.
calendar.author: Omar Sakka
calendar.name: calendar

contacts.title: Contacts
contacts.about:
The people in your address books, kept offline from CardDAV

the people in your address books, kept on this machine from a CardDAV server (Nextcloud, Fastmail, iCloud, Radicale, anything standard): a list down the left, searchable, and the person chosen on the right -- their emails, any of which writes them a message in Mail, their phones, address, organisation and note. n adds someone, e or enter edits, # or delete removes, / searches, j and k move, R syncs now.

Which servers are used is Control Panel > PIM, from the Servers list; each is kept under ~/.local/share/hibr/pim/SERVER by lib/pimsync.hibr, run in the background -- the only thing that writes there. A change made here is made to the list at once and queued for the server, conditional on the copy it was read from; the next sync sends it. Mail reads the same copies to finish an address as it is typed.
contacts.author: Omar Sakka
contacts.name: contacts

files.title: Files
files.about:
A file browser for the desktop, and a lister on its own.

    hibr programs/desktop/apps/files.hibr /etc
files.author: Omar Sakka
files.name: files

switchboard.title: Switchboard
switchboard.about:
Watch a longwire switchboard: who is on it and who is ringing whom

a window on a longwire switchboard you run: how many nodes are on it, which of them are online, and who is ringing whom right now. It reads the switchboard's own worker through `lw`, once a second, and follows its event stream for the calls. It watches; it does not decide anything (a ring and a registration are the script's to answer, and the script has two seconds). The head says what this switchboard is and whether anything needs looking at (a key cut to 30 characters says neither): its short code, how long it has been up, its policy and version, how full it is, and a line for what is wrong. Its full address, which a node's `--switchboard HOST:PORT/ADDRESS` needs, is one key away (a, or Node > Copy Switchboard Address). `m` makes the head compact: no graphs, one line for the rest (docs/adr/0075).

Traffic in and out, the calls since it started, and the bans are on its head; `/` searches the nodes by number or name, `o` shows only those online, `b` turns the list into the bans (and `x` lifts one, for the switchboard's owner). Every key is in the menus (docs/adr/0049).
switchboard.author: Omar Sakka
switchboard.name: switchboard

term.title: Terminal
term.about:
A shell in a window, which is the last step of decision 0020.

The window manager hands this app a rectangle and some keys; the term module runs a program on a pseudo terminal, keeps a picture of its screen and paints that picture into the rectangle. What runs inside is a real program with a real terminal: it edits its own line, draws its own colours and does not know it is in a window.
term.author: Omar Sakka
term.name: term

vault.title: Vault
vault.about:
The Bitwarden or Vaultwarden vault's items, found by typing

a desk accessory (Gitea #71): the Bitwarden or Vaultwarden vault's items, found by typing, and a password, a username or a TOTP code copied for a while. Unlocking, locking and syncing are the desktop's own (wm/vault.hibr), so the window, Control Panel > Passwords and every Terminal opened after an unlock agree on whether it is open.
vault.author: Omar Sakka
vault.name: vault

about.title: About This Computer
about.about:
About this computer: the machine, and the desktop running on it

what this is, and what it is running on.

On Linux the machine's own numbers come from /proc, read directly and costing no fork, the same way mods/sysinfo does in C. Nothing else keeps a /proc, so everywhere else forks a system command instead -- vm_stat and sysctl for memory, top for CPU, both throttled to AB_SLOWMS since forking a command every frame is not something to do at DT_TICK's pace. A window rather than the one-line note it used to be, because a bar that means something has to keep being redrawn, and a note fades on its own.
about.author: Omar Sakka
about.name: about

catalogue.title: Catalogue
catalogue.about:
The application catalogue: browse, install, update and remove

the Catalogue window: the catalogue in a window. The `catalogue` command is the whole implementation and this is a window around it, the way the Vault accessory is a window around `vw` -- anything one can do the other can, because there is only one of them (Gitea #219).

It reads `catalogue list -j`, never the columns `catalogue` prints for a person: the command answers JSON for exactly this, so the window and the command read one answer instead of one parsing the other's layout. Parsing a layout is how a window comes to disagree with its own command.
catalogue.author: Omar Sakka
catalogue.name: catalogue

clipboard.title: Clipboard
clipboard.about:
The clipboard's history: copy something back, pin it, keep it

the clipboard's history, newest first (wm/clip.hibr keeps it). Each line is when it was copied, a ★ if pinned, a • on what is on the clipboard now, and the start of the text. Enter makes the selected one the clipboard again; p pins it, so it is never dropped; delete takes it away. A paste into this window -- alt-v, or the machine's own -- keeps what was pasted, to come back to later; Copy takes the selected one.
clipboard.author: Omar Sakka
clipboard.name: clipboard

modman.title: Modules
modman.about:
What this shell can load, what it has loaded, and a way to change either

Modules: what this shell can load, what it has loaded, and a way to change either (#133).

Everything here is `mod avail`'s own answer: it walks the module path and reads each object's descriptor *without calling its init*, so a module can be named, versioned and described before it is ever loaded. In a pipe that answer is one line of eight tab-separated fields per module, which is what this reads -- never the column form, which is for a person.
modman.author: Omar Sakka
modman.name: modman

notifications.title: Notifications
notifications.about:
A read-only look back at recent notifications

a look back at what DT_NOTEHIST kept: newest first, each note's time, priority, sender and text. Up and down select one, delete clears it, and the History menu clears the low ones or all of them.

Opened directly by the menu bar's icon (dt_bar in wm/bar.hibr, dt_mouse in wm/input.hibr) and by the Notifications pane's own "View History" row, never from a generic Applications pick -- hidden, the same reason About and Process Details are: nothing about "show me what already happened" makes sense launched with no history behind it, though here an empty one just shows an empty list rather than being refused.
notifications.author: Omar Sakka
notifications.name: notifications

screenshot.title: Screenshot…
screenshot.about:
Take a screenshot of the screen, a window or an area

the desk accessory that takes one: Screenshot… asks Screen, Window or Area, the same as its shortcut (wm/shot.hibr does the taking). It opens no window of its own, so it gives screenshot_launch and nothing else; the Image Viewer, beside it, is what shows an .ans one afterwards.
screenshot.author: Omar Sakka
screenshot.name: screenshot

tasks.title: Task Manager
tasks.about:
What is running, and a way to end one of them.

On Linux, reads /proc directly, the same technique mods/mon and the about window both use: no forking, and no dependency on anything but the kernel giving a truthful /proc. Elsewhere, one ps -axo per scan, since there is no /proc to read there at all -- ps already computes %CPU itself, so there is no delta of its own to keep between scans, unlike the Linux path. Sorted by CPU or memory, x or Task > End Task sends the selected one SIGTERM, shift-x sends SIGKILL.
tasks.author: Omar Sakka
tasks.name: tasks

aboutme.title: About Me
aboutme.about: The Control Panel pane for About Me: the name, the line under it and the picture the login screen shows for you (programs/desktop/login/), and which session it starts. They live in ~/.config/hibr/me.json -- data, never run, since the login screen reads it before anyone has logged in (as you, never as root). The picture is a PNG or JPEG anywhere you can read it; the file keeps its path.
aboutme.author: Omar Sakka
aboutme.name: aboutme

appearance.title: Appearance
appearance.about: The Control Panel pane for how the desktop looks: the theme (the whole look at once), the colour scheme, the glyphs and trees, the shadows, and how dialog buttons look. The menu bar has a pane of its own since 0.99.356 (menubar.hibr, Gitea #396), its look and its items. The wallpaper has a pane of its own since 0.99.246 (wallset.hibr, Gitea #284), though a theme still carries one and applies it here. A theme or a colour scheme sets the variables the window manager already reads every frame, so a change shows on the next one, in every window at once.
appearance.author: Omar Sakka
appearance.name: appearance

arabizi.title: Arabizi
arabizi.about:
The Control Panel pane for Arabizi, from hibr-ime

tuning Arabizi, the input method hibr-ime brings: whether it writes tashkeel, which letter each Arabizi digit reads as, the person's own words, and a box to try it in. It writes only the person's own layer, $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/hibr/ime/arabizi/ -- `options`, and `arabizi.rules` in the shipped rules' own format, read after them -- which hibr's ime module and Blit's compositor both read, so a program window and a desktop field always convert alike. A line of that file the pane does not manage is kept as it is.

blit.title: Blit
blit.about:
API configuration and diagnostics for the Blit display server.

Auxiliary Apply changes the running policy; Save as Default writes Blit's existing settings resource with revision protection. Login preferences take effect at restart. Font changes use Blit's live-and-saved font API. Hibr Displays continues to own native desktop arrangement after initial attachment. Every network request is hibr's own dav request, in a bounded background job of the desktop's (dt_job); no curl, and the token never on a command line. The connection token is kept in a private user file, is masked in its editor, and is excluded from configuration exports. The privileged updater token is never requested. The source of this pane is this file, in the hibr catalogue (itdlabs/hibr-apps), not the Blit tree.
blit.author: Omar Sakka
blit.name: blit

control-strip.title: Control Strip
control-strip.about: The Control Panel pane for the strip itself: which side it docks to, and whether it casts its own shadow, the same reasoning as Behaviour's own Window Shadow and Menu Shadow rows. Position, collapse and length are dragged directly on the strip, the same as a window is moved and resized on itself rather than from a settings row -- this pane only carries the two things that are otherwise nowhere to see or change.
control-strip.author: Omar Sakka
control-strip.name: control-strip

datetime.title: Date & Time
datetime.about:
The Control Panel pane for the time, the date and the time zone

the Control Panel pane for the time, the date, and a small world map with a mark near the machine's own time zone, System 7's Date & Time control panel. A custom pane, since a map needs a body of its own rather than two columns of text.

The map data, its scoring, and the zone1970.tab lookup are all copied from examples/traceroute.hibr rather than redone: CLAUDE.md's own trap about that map says not to adjust one by eye, and the same is true of drawing a second one. What is copied is copied unchanged; only the projection's target size differs, since this map is a corner of a settings pane and not a full screen.
datetime.author: Omar Sakka
datetime.name: datetime

desktop.title: Desktop
desktop.about: The Control Panel pane for the bare desktop: which icons sit on it, how many workspaces it has, whether Cycle goes through this one's windows or every one's, how often a busy screen is redrawn, and how screenshots are taken and where they go.
desktop.author: Omar Sakka
desktop.name: desktop

displays.title: Displays
displays.about: Control Panel's own picture of a multi-monitor arrangement: a dropdown to choose which display is primary, and every attached display drawn to scale below it from hold clients, dragged to reposition (hold move on release). Right-click a rectangle for Detach (hold drop) or Identify (flash its own name on its own screen, so whoever is looking can tell which is which). The primary display is the picture's own anchor -- every rectangle is positioned relative to it, so switching which one is primary, or dragging a *different* display, never moves where the primary itself draws -- but its own rectangle cannot be dragged: the dropdown is the one reliable way to change it, since a mouse click precise enough to land on a specific terminal cell with *no* movement at all is not something to depend on, over ssh least of all. Nothing else is kept that a fresh read of hold clients cannot recompute -- the same as every other pane's row list is rebuilt every frame -- except the drag itself, which is this window's own gesture in progress and belongs nowhere else, and is frozen against hold clients while it is happening: re-reading mid-drag would have the dragged rectangle's own base position shift under the live preview the moment the release this same drag ends in reaches the server.
displays.author: Omar Sakka
displays.name: displays

filetypes.title: File Types
filetypes.about:
Which program opens which kind of file

the Control Panel pane for dt_handler's own extension-to- program table (DT_HANDLERS). Files' own Open With menu already reads it; this is where a mapping is added, changed or removed, rather than only through a dt_handler line in a script of your own -- which still works exactly as before, and is what dt_save now writes these back out as.
filetypes.author: Omar Sakka
filetypes.name: filetypes

language.title: Language & Region
language.about:
The system's language and region, and how the desktop shows them

the Control Panel pane for Language & Region (Gitea #526): the system's language, which programs speak and the desktop's own words follow wherever hibr has a catalogue (#68, ADR 0032), and its region, the formats programs write dates, numbers, money, measures and paper in, each of which may be set on its own. They are the system's, one source of truth: read from it and changed through localectl, which asks for an administrator (wm/locale.hibr). Below them, how the desktop itself shows right-to-left text and digits.
language.author: Omar Sakka
language.name: language

loginmgr.title: Login Manager
loginmgr.about:
The Control Panel pane for the login screen

Control Panel > Login Manager (Gitea #389): how hibr's login screen looks and what it offers, and where it runs.

Its settings are /etc/hibr/login.json, root's file, which the screen reads once when it starts. This pane reads it as you -- it is readable by everyone -- and changes it through hibr-loginset under pkexec, hibr's action org.hibr.loginscreen, which Administrative Access governs like any other: changes wait, marked, until Apply Changes, so several cost one password. A theme, a colour scheme and a saver are offered only from what the screen itself can read, which is what hibr ships and the system scope -- never anybody's home, since the screen is root.
loginmgr.author: Omar Sakka
loginmgr.name: loginmgr

menubar.title: Menu Bar
menubar.about:
The Control Panel pane for the menu bar: how it looks -- the gap between its items, how much of a picture shows through it, the notification icon, its shadow, bold titles and how wide a menu may grow -- and what is on it, Menu Bar Items, every item on its right ticked on or off and dragged into the order it reads in (Gitea #396). These were Appearance's own Menu Bar rows until 0.99.356; the settings are the same ones, so nothing saved moves.

The pane is called barset, not menubar: dt_menubar is the window manager's own loader, and a pane's name is the prefix its callbacks are looked up by.
menubar.author: Omar Sakka
menubar.name: menubar

menuedit.title: Applications Menu
menuedit.about:
The Control Panel pane for what the Applications menu holds

Control Panel > Applications Menu (Gitea #502): what the Applications menu holds besides the desktop's own apps. The programs installed on the machine are listed by themselves (wm/programs.hibr), each a row here that opens to change it, or Hide to take it off the menu; Add Program makes one of the person's own -- a name, a command, the folder under Applications it goes in, and whether it runs in a window of its own or in a Terminal window. What is changed here is the person's, kept as data in $XDG_DATA_HOME/hibr/menu.json, and wins over the machine's. Replaces Screens and its pane (owner, 2026-11-10). The dialog is pmfield.
menuedit.author: Omar Sakka
menuedit.name: menuedit

mouse.title: Mouse
mouse.about: The Control Panel pane for what the mouse does to a window: whether a plain side resizes it as well as a corner, whether a modifier click anywhere in its body moves it and which modifier, and what a double click on its title bar does, whether a dragged window follows by its outline or whole, how far one notch of the wheel scrolls, and whether and how soon a tooltip shows. wm/input.hibr reads the window settings and every scrolling window the wheel's; this pane only changes the DT_* settings.
mouse.author: Omar Sakka
mouse.name: mouse

networks.title: Network
networks.about:
The Control Panel pane for the machine's network and Wi-Fi

the Control Panel pane called Network (Gitea #311): what the machine is on and its address, Wi-Fi on or off, the networks in reach to join, the ones it knows to forget, and the item on the menu bar. It acts through menubar/network.hibr, which says how this machine is networked: NetworkManager, or iproute2's view alone.

The pane is called networks, not network, on purpose: network is the WebDAV servers' pane (titled Servers), shipped and in the catalogue, and a copy of it installed in a person's own scope would win over a shipped file of the same name -- so a new pane there would be shadowed by an old one.
networks.author: Omar Sakka
networks.name: networks

pictures.title: Pictures
pictures.about:
The Control Panel pane for how a picture is drawn: half blocks, the same in grey, the character ramp, or real pixels where the terminal can place them. One setting reaches every picture the desktop draws -- the Image Viewer, the wallpaper, Mail's pictures, the film player and the browser -- since each passes DT_IMGMODE to the module that draws it.

What the terminal can do is shown beside it, because the honest answer is "it depends on your terminal", and it names the protocol in force: the kitty graphics protocol or sixel, each needing the terminal to say what a cell measures (ADR 0037). Which of the two is not a choice -- no terminal does both well, and kitty does not do sixel at all -- so the setting says Pixels and the console picks.
pictures.author: Omar Sakka
pictures.name: pictures

pnotes.title: Program Notifications
pnotes.about:
Programs' notifications as the desktop's own, switched in Notifications

programs' notifications as the desktop's own (Gitea #505): a catalogue entry, not part of the package (the owner, 2026-11-15). The listener alone: its switch is a row of Notifications, which shows it while this is installed, since a pane of its own beside Notifications was a second place for the same notes (the owner, 2026-11-15, 0.99.536). Installed and switched on, the desktop is the session's org.freedesktop.Notifications, through the dbus module and wm/bus.hibr: what a program says becomes one of the desktop's notes -- the same stack, history, per-app rules and Do Not Disturb -- under the program's own name, at a priority from its urgency. A click runs the program's default action (or its first); a note the program replaces is replaced; one it closes goes; and the program is told when each has gone, by a click or its time running out. Another program already the session's notification server keeps the name, and the log says so.

Removed while the desktop runs, it lets the name go (dt_onunload), so the notifications go back to whatever else the session has.
pnotes.author: Omar Sakka
pnotes.name: pnotes

screensaver.title: Screen Saver
screensaver.about: The Control Panel pane for the screen saver (wm/saver.hibr): which one, or one at random, how many idle minutes before it starts, whether it locks the screen (wm/lock.hibr) once it has run a while, and a look at it now.
screensaver.author: Omar Sakka
screensaver.name: screensaver

shortcuts.title: Shortcuts
shortcuts.about: The Control Panel pane for every shortcut in one list: the desktop's own actions, then a launch shortcut for any app, then each app's own actions. A shortcut is the chords it is written as (ADR 0057): activating a row captures its next key as its only one; its + captures one more beside those it has; the ✕ beside a key, or delete or backspace on its row, clears them. wm/keys.hibr does all of it -- including asking before taking a key another action has, and refusing one Blit keeps for itself, which are listed last. Every key the desktop acts on is here, the menu bar's, Copy's, Cut's and Paste's included. A key two actions share, which only a settings file edited by hand can arrange, is marked ⚠ on both. Use Super Instead of Alt, and back, rewrite the list once.
shortcuts.author: Omar Sakka
shortcuts.name: shortcuts

versions.title: Versions
versions.about: Which image each part of this desktop is actually running. About This Computer cannot answer that: it draws $HIBR_VERSION, which is the *desktop process's* own version, and a restart replaces that process and every module it loads while leaving the hold server's image exactly as old as the session (Gitea #42, #198). Three states, asked and named separately, because they move independently.
versions.author: Omar Sakka
versions.name: versions

wallset.title: Wallpaper
wallset.about:
The Control Panel pane for the wallpaper of each display

the Control Panel pane for the wallpaper: the pattern, or an image chosen in a picker of its own (control-panel/wallpaper.hibr), how it fills the screen, and how it is drawn -- for every display at once, or for one display by its name (Gitea #284). It was a section of Appearance until then; it is a pane of its own because a Display row choosing what every row below it applies to reads plainly here, and would not among Appearance's rows, which all apply everywhere.

A display is known by the name it attached under: --name if it was given one, otherwise the machine it connects from (dt_dispname), so a reattach finds it again. One with a wallpaper of its own keeps it in DT_WALLDIMG, DT_WALLDMODE and DT_WALLDPIC (wm/wallpaper.hibr); one with none follows All Displays, which is DT_WALLIMG, DT_WALLMODE and DT_WALLIMGMODE as before -- so a settings file written before this pane existed means exactly what it did. The pattern is one for the whole desktop, and is only offered under All Displays.
wallset.author: Omar Sakka
wallset.name: wallset

windows.title: Windows
windows.about:
The Control Panel pane for how a window looks and where it opens

the Control Panel pane for how a window looks and where a new one goes: its frame, where its title sits, which glyphs the buttons are drawn with, the Title Bar Buttons list -- each button on or off, and on which side of the title -- Placement, what Zoom fills -- the window's own display or every display (Gitea #286) -- and how wide a tiled workspace's main window is. How the mouse moves, resizes and double-clicks one is the Mouse pane's. Every value here is read by wm/frame.hibr; this pane only ever changes the DT_* settings, never the drawing itself.
windows.author: Omar Sakka
windows.name: windows

cursor.title: Cursor
cursor.about: A Control Strip module for a new terminal's cursor style, the same DT_CURSOR setting Behaviour's own Cursor row changes. Its own name rather than a shape or a letter -- a click opens the three styles as a dropdown, the same as Behaviour's own Cursor row does from a click on its value, so the current style is seen and chosen in the same place.
cursor.author: Omar Sakka
cursor.name: cursor

shadow.title: Shadow
shadow.about: A Control Strip module toggling window shadows, the same DT_SHADOW setting Behaviour's own Window Shadow row changes. Its own name, not a glyph -- bold in the active colour when on, dimmed when off, since a single icon read as nothing in particular to anyone who had not already memorised what it meant.
shadow.author: Omar Sakka
shadow.name: shadow

theme.title: Theme
theme.about:
A Control Strip module cycling the desktop's colour theme

a Control Strip module cycling the desktop's own colour theme, by its own name rather than a first letter or a swatch -- a click opens every theme as a dropdown, reusing Appearance's own cp_theme() and CP_THEMES rather than a second copy of the list of themes. If Control Panel is not loaded there is nothing to offer, so a click does nothing, honestly, rather than switching only some of the colours.
theme.author: Omar Sakka
theme.name: theme

wallpaper.title: Wallpaper
wallpaper.about: A Control Strip module cycling the desktop's own wallpaper glyph, the same DT_GLYPH setting Appearance's own Wallpaper row changes. Its own name, not the glyph itself -- a click opens every glyph as a dropdown, each shown as itself, which is its own preview.
wallpaper.author: Omar Sakka
wallpaper.name: wallpaper

workspaces.title: Workspaces
workspaces.about: A Control Strip module for the workspace numbers, the same ones the menu bar can show (menubar/workspaces.hibr): the current one lit, a click on another goes there. The strip and the bar can each show them, or both, or neither (Gitea #393).
workspaces.author: Omar Sakka
workspaces.name: workspaces

classicmac.title: Classic Mac
classicmac.about: A compact Macintosh drifting slowly about a dark screen, its little screen going through what one did: the happy face it started with, then the desktop -- a menu bar, a disk, a trash -- then a window opening on it, and round again.
classicmac.author: Omar Sakka
classicmac.name: classicmac

matrix.title: Matrix
matrix.about:
Green rain: glyphs falling down every column of the screen

green rain: a column of glyphs falls down each column of the screen, each at its own speed and length, its head bright, the trail behind it greener and then darker, until it falls off the bottom and starts again somewhere above the top.
matrix.author: Omar Sakka
matrix.name: matrix

mystify.title: Mystify
mystify.about: Two four-cornered shapes bouncing about the screen, each corner on its own course, leaving a short trail of themselves behind, their colours slowly turning.
mystify.author: Omar Sakka
mystify.name: mystify

pipes.title: Pipes
pipes.about: Pipes growing across the screen a joint at a time, turning now and then, each its own colour, until the screen is full of them and it starts again.
pipes.author: Omar Sakka
pipes.name: pipes

toasters.title: Flying Toasters
toasters.about: Flying toasters, in the old After Dark way: toasters flapping their wings and slices of toast drifting down and to the left across a black sky, each at its own pace, coming round again from the top and the right.
toasters.author: Omar Sakka
toasters.name: toasters

longwire-switchboard.title: longwire-switchboard
longwire-switchboard.about:

the switchboard (component 1). The module's C worker runs the mechanism (sessions, presence, introductions); this script is the policy: who may register, and whose call may ring. See docs/SWITCHBOARD.md.

video-bilibili.title: video-bilibili
video-bilibili.about:
Video: Bilibili, a site for the Video player

Bilibili (bilibili.com) for the Video player (apps/video): what only Bilibili knows. A provider lib (kind `lib`): it adds itself to VIDEO_SITES, and the app calls its functions by their prefix, vb_. Bilibili's lists are its own public pages of data (the popular list, a search), which the engine loads like any page and the app reads, after one visit to the site in the window (a search is refused without its cookies). A video is looked up in two steps -- its part, then its file, an MP4 of 720p or 360p that expires, so it is asked for each time one starts -- and played in a small page of this lib's own with one <video> in it. A file the engine cannot reach or play never says so (it stalls): the player gives a title up after thirty seconds. Only ids that look like Bilibili's (BV and letters and digits) are played.
video-bilibili.author: Omar Sakka
video-bilibili.name: video-bilibili

video-bilibilitv.title: video-bilibilitv
video-bilibilitv.about:
Video: Bilibili TV, a site for the Video player

Bilibili TV (bilibili.tv, the international site) for the Video player (apps/video): what only it knows. A provider lib (kind `lib`): it adds itself to VIDEO_SITES, and the app calls its functions by their prefix, vq_. Its lists (the home page, a search) are the site's own pages, read from their links: a title's id is the number in the link and its words are its picture's text. A video is looked up in one step, the site's own data service (the page the site's player asks it for, loaded in the player tab as a page and read): it answers with the address of an MP4 file, which is played in a small page of this lib's own with one <video> in it. (The site's own player, in a window that is not shown, does not start; the file itself plays and seeks.) A file that does not come is given up on by the player after twenty-five seconds, one that does not play after thirty, and the window says so. Only ids that are numbers are played.

video-bilibilitv.name: video-bilibilitv

video-tubi.title: video-tubi
video-tubi.about:
Video: Tubi, a site for the Video player

Tubi (tubitv.com) for the Video player (apps/video): what only Tubi knows. A provider lib (kind `lib`): it adds itself to VIDEO_SITES, and the app calls its functions by their prefix, vt_. Tubi's lists (the home page, a search, a series and its seasons) are read from the page's own links; a title is Tubi's page for it, cut down to its one <video> once that holds data. A title that Tubi protects with DRM cannot be played by this engine, and the player says so rather than waiting.

video-youtube.title: video-youtube
video-youtube.about:
Video: YouTube, a site for the Video player

YouTube (youtube.com) for the Video player (apps/video): what only YouTube knows. A provider lib (kind `lib`): it adds itself to VIDEO_SITES, and the app calls its functions by their prefix, vy_. YouTube's lists (a search, a playlist, a channel) are its own pages' data (ytInitialData), read once the page has made it; a title is YouTube's watch page, which the engine plays itself, cut down to its one <video>; the player is driven through YouTube's own (movie_player) calls. What only YouTube has is here: its adverts (their time and length are not the video's), a page that goes on to another video by itself (followed), its own autoplay switch (turned off, the player's Play Next Automatically is the one), the qualities it offers and its captions.

videocore.title: videocore
videocore.about:
The video apps' shared core: history, favourites and library lines

what the video apps (YouTube, Tubi, Bilibili, and the ones after them) share: the history and favourites files, the line of the shared video library (docs/video-library.md of the catalogue), the reading of a line, and a time as 1:05. Provider-free: it knows no site and no window, and holds nothing of an app's state; each app keeps its own names (`yt_fileput`, `tu_libput`, ...) as thin calls into this, so what the apps and their tests use does not move.

A library of the catalogue (kind `lib`): installed to <scope>/lib/videocore.hibr, read by the desktop at start (it is chosen by the line below), and named by an app with `# needs: lib/videocore`. Entries are updated apart, and `needs:` carries no version, so the core has its own: VC_API. An app asks `vc_ok N` when it opens and says so in its window when the core is not there or is older than it needs; it never half-works.
videocore.author: Omar Sakka
videocore.name: videocore
